publisher.title: The Times of India
full_article:
Dhrubajyoti Guha, based near Frankfurt in Germany, graduated in mechanical engineering from Bengal Engineering College, Shibpur (now IIEST Shibpur), in 2002.

TOI



Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.



An Indian-origin climber and his Nepalese Sherpa guide were killed in an overnight avalanche at Camp 3 on Mount Manaslu (8,163m) after they continued towards the summit while six other climbers turned back amid worsening weather, expedition organisers said on Sunday. Rescuers found Dhrubajyoti Guha and Fursemba Sherpa, both 47, buried inside their tent, taking the autumn season toll on the world’s eighth-highest peak to four.Guha, based near Frankfurt in Germany, graduated in mechanical engineering from Bengal Engineering College, Shibpur (now IIEST Shibpur), in 2002. He had worked with ABB, IBM, Pfizer and Nestlé and was an accomplished ultra-endurance trail runner with 32 UTMB World Series race finishes, including several over 100km. Sherpa was an NMA-registered guide from Nepal’s Makalu region who had summited Everest nine times and also climbed Kangchenjunga, Lhotse, Cho Oyu and Manaslu.Mohan Lamsal, managing director of expedition organiser Makalu Adventure, said conditions deteriorated as the group reached the higher camps. “Six other climbers who decided to retreat from Camp 2 are safe, but Guha and Sherpa decided to make an early summit attempt and headed for Camp III on Saturday evening,” Lamsal toldContact with the two was lost overnight. “We were alerted around 11.30am on Sunday after they stopped responding. We immediately sent four Sherpa climbers to Camp III to look for them. They dug through the snow and found both inside their tent, buried beneath nearly seven feet of snow,” Lamsal said.Continuing snowfall and avalanche risk prevented the rescuers from bringing the bodies to base camp. “I asked the rescue team to descend to the lower camps because it was not safe to remain there. We will try to bring the bodies down once the weather improves,” Lamsal said.Heavy snowfall began on Friday evening and continued through Sunday, with up to 60cm recorded at base camp, forcing hundreds of climbers to retreat or remain at lower camps. Some teams had begun ascending on Saturday in anticipation of a relatively favourable weather window from Monday, but meteorologists had warned of another spell of bad weather around Wednesday as a system developing over the Bay of Bengal was expected to affect the region.The deaths followed two earlier fatalities on Manaslu this autumn. Singaporean climber Lau Wee Seng, 50, died at around 6,000m while descending from Camp 2 on Sept 17, while Tashi Sherpa, 20, a Nepali high-altitude worker, was found dead inside a tent at base camp on Sept 5.Manaslu has drawn a record 480 foreign climbers this autumn, accompanied by more than 500 Nepali guides and support staff. The latest fatalities took the number of reported mountaineering deaths across the Himalayas and Karakoram this year to at least 24, making 2026 one of the deadliest for climbers in the region in recent years.

title: Photos: Nepal flood survivors find little trace of former lives - Al Jazeera
description: Photos: Nepal flood survivors find little trace of former lives  Al Jazeera
publisher.title: Al Jazeera
full_article:
When Anusa Thapa Magar rushed home from her job in the Maldives after hearing of Nepal’s devastating floods, she clung to the hope that her grandmother had somehow survived.

Instead, when she reached Betrawati, the small riverside town where her family lived, she found only a flat expanse of hardened grey silt.

There was no house, and no Betrawati.

“If my house is buried underneath, that means my Aama is still here underneath too, right?” the 23-year-old said quietly, standing where the family’s two-storey home once stood. Her grandmother, who could barely walk, was last seen resting on her bed.

Last month’s torrent of mud, rock and water, triggered by a glacial collapse in the mountains along the Nepal-China border, tore through settlements along the Trishuli River, killing at least 1,386 people on the Nepal side. Authorities say 5,130 are still missing, and while searches continue, it has been days since anyone was found alive.

To reach what used to be Betrawati, survivors now climb a steep hillside, cross a narrow ridge and descend into a wasteland. Along the route lie scattered shoes, school ties and children’s backpacks – “silent evidence”, residents say, of the panic as people scrambled to flee the surging floodwaters.

Garment business owner Kalpana Thapa Magar, 43, recalled the moment a friend phoned from upstream. “Run! Run!” she was told. “I just ran. When I looked back, everything was gone, even the people who had been running behind me,” she said.

Downstream in Devighat, shattered shells of houses still stand. Some residents pick through the rubble for belongings, but many say there is no reason to return; the land itself has vanished beneath debris.

Advertisement

For many here, the disaster reopens wounds from Nepal’s 2015 earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people. Teacher Sita Thapa Magar, 45, Kalpana’s older sister, said that after the quake, families were at least able to rebuild on their plots. “This time, we have lost everything,” she said. “Our houses, our land, our future.”

On a single broken floor tile – the last visible trace of her home – 61-year-old Shanti Dangol clutched a photograph of the three-storey lodge she once ran for pilgrims and trekkers.

“Economically, people here had started doing well,” she said. “Now, nothing remains.”

Concealed within an artificial hill in Jakarta, the Chicken Hero Pavilion by RAD+ar is an ingenious bamboo chicken coop. Anjung, Malaysia, by Eleena Jamil

Near Kuala Lumpur, Eleena Jamil’s Anjung uses bamboo and green-painted steel to shelter a family guesthouse and studio. title: Nepal's Gen Z is taking on the world's polluters over climate disasters - Business Standard
description: Nepal's Gen Z is taking on the world's polluters over climate disasters  Business Standard
publisher.title: Business Standard
full_article:
By Hannah Beech & Sajal Pradhan

When Tashi Lhazom was 11, a glacial lake overflowed and inundated her home in a high Himalayan valley. Of her fami- ly’s hundreds of shaggy yaks, only two survived. In 2025, another flash flood cascaded into the village, the result, scientists say, of melting permafrost on a warming planet.

Such natural disasters spurred Lhazom’s political awakening. When Nepali young people protested a year ago, she joined other climate activists on the forefront of a Gen Z revolution that eventually ushered in a youth-dominated government in March.

Last month, when a glacial collapse created an inland tsunami that left more than 8,000 dead or missing in other Hima layan valleys in Nepal and Tibet, Lhazom again raised her voice. Now 26, she dema- nded that the world’s most polluting countries compensate Nepal for what she calls a “climate national emergency.”

“It’s high time we shift from the language of foreign aid to the language of climate compensation and even reparations,” she said.

Also Read Nepal flood death toll crosses 1,450; over 6,000 people still missing India's 'neighbourhood first' policy gets a boost amid diplomatic push India, Nepal discuss ways to facilitate legitimate trade and transit Nepal flash floods death toll crosses 1400, over 6,100 people still missing Google picks 4 Indian startups for inaugural DeepMind AI accelerator

After the August 26 floods, the Nepali government has made climate justice its global calling card. Next week, Balendra Shah, the 36-year-old prime minister of Nepal, is expected to address the United Nations General Assembly and push for industrialised powers to foot the bills faced by lesser-developed countries disproportionately affected by climate-linked disasters. The prime minister’s office is now in close contact with Greta Thunberg, the young campaigner who made a video supporting Nepal’s quest for climate reparations. Whether Nepal can persuade industrialised powers to make climate reparations is far from certain — and there is no consensus on which nations should pay.

Under President Trump, the United States, historically the world’s largest polluter, has distanced itself from climate science and the multilateral institutions that could provide a path for compensation. China and India, currently the first- and third-la- rgest producers of greenhouse gases, chafe at being held liable for what they say are the sins of less populous Western nations that polluted with impunity for centuries. Geographically, Nepal is wedged between India and China.

“That’s one of the trickiest and most challenging conversations, not just for Nepal, but in a broader climate discourse,” Khanal said, when asked which heavy carbon emitters should be liable for climate-linked catastrophes striking smaller, poorer countries.

Nepal has put the initial price tag for flood recovery and reconstruction at $4.74 billion. The nation is still paying off loans for international assistance from an earthquake 11 years ago. During his appearance before the General Assembly in New York next week, Shah will have to balance an urgent appeal on behalf of the world’s least-developed nations with a charm campaign toward richer countries that may not appreciate being targeted for climate compensation.

This year, the Nepali government was provisionally allocated about $20 million from a special UN fund for nations vulnerable to climate change, according to Nepali officials. But an emergency request that the Nepali government made after the floods has yet to receive a reply.

A week after the flooding, Gita Chaudhary, Nepal’s envi- ronment minister, represented her country at a meeting of the 44 nations recogn- ised by the United Nations as least developed, where she pushed for climate financing. Chaudhary, 33, is from an Indigenous community and grew up in what is now a national park.

The science, climate experts say, is straightforward. Unlike its giant Asian neighbors, Nepal produces a negligible wisp of greenhouse gases. Nearly all of its energy generation comes from hydropower. The country is importing fleets of electric vehicles from China. More than 45 percent of the country is forested, and that green cover is increasing, courtesy of community management programs.

Chaudhary, 33, is from an Indigenous community and grew up in what is now a national park.

“Historical emitters need to be held accountable,” Chaudhary said in an interview, referring to Western nations, adding that current ones, such as India and China, bore responsibility, too.

description: Leadership dispute in Nepal's UML intensifies — Kathmandu Post  ua.news
publisher.title: ua.news
full_article:
In Nepal, an internal party dispute in the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist), or CPN-UML, has escalated from a discussion about organizational changes into a challenge to party chair K. P. Sharma Oli. After the March 5 elections, which were unsuccessful for the party, a number of senior CPN-UML leaders called for changes to policy, structure and approaches to leadership transition, Kathmandu Post reports.

General Secretary Shankar Pokhrel proposed that Oli himself initiate a leadership transition as part of a broader party reorganization. Oli rejected the idea. At the same time, the party's task force decided not to include the issue of leadership change in its consolidated report, instead adding proposals from provincial structures and other bodies as an appendix.

The issue will be considered by the Central Committee

Deputy General Secretary Lekhraj Bhatta said that the issue of leadership change would be discussed by the Central Committee rather than considered as a recommendation in the task force report. The party Secretariat also decided to propose holding a meeting of the National General Convention Representatives Council.

The discussion intensified after 13 provincial and organizational meetings, at which the party collected assessments of the election results and its future course. Pokhrel, who served as secretary of the task force led by Vice Chair Ram Bahadur Thapa, prepared a report calling for large-scale reorganization. According to the publication, most provincial units, with the exception of Bagmati, proposed changing the party's policy and leadership.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Different approaches to reorganization

In his separate report, Thapa considered it premature to raise the issue of leadership transition during a crisis and denied a link between party reorganization and Oli's removal. Pokhrel, Vice Chair Bishnu Paudel, Gokarna Bista and Yogesh Bhattarai disagreed with his position. Later, Pradeep Gyawali prepared a third document intended to reconcile the different positions.

Oli refers to the mandate received at the party's 11th General Convention in December 2025. Under Clause 72 of the CPN-UML statute, convening an extraordinary General Convention requires a written demand from two-thirds of district committees or a majority of members of the Representatives Council. There were 2,263 representatives at the 11th convention, meaning at least 1,132 people are needed for such a demand.

In September 2025, the party abolished the 70-year age limit for senior party positions, allowing Oli to run for another term. Pokhrel explained the need for changes by the need to establish a mechanism for the consistent development and transition of leadership between different generations.

title: Mixed fortunes for Nepal on Day Two Karateka Gurung misses out on podium - The Rising Nepal
description: Mixed fortunes for Nepal on Day Two Karateka Gurung misses out on podium  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By Pramod Joshi

Nagoya, Sept. 21: Arika Gurung, one of Nepal's most accomplished karate players and a silver medalist at the 19th Asian Games, entered the continental event with high expectations of ending the nation's gold drought. However, the weight of expectation proved heavy as she finished without a medal.

Gurung began her campaign at Toyohashi Gymnasium by defeating Jordan's Yara Naser 7-1, courtesy of three waza-ari and a yuko. The victory set up a semi-final clash with familiar rival Sofya Berultseva of Kazakhstan, the world number one in the women's +68kg kumite.

Berultseva, who defeated Gurung in the 19th Asiad final, once again proved a stumbling block, securing a 2-1 victory. Aside from a semi-final win against the world number one at the 20th Asian Karate Championship, Gurung has previously fallen to Berultseva in the WKF Karate 1 Premier League finals in Istanbul and Leshan this year.

Relegated to the bronze-medal match, Gurung suffered a narrow 8-7 defeat to Saudi Arabia's Dina Ahmed Mostafa. The Saudi competitor collected two points from a yuko and two ippon, while Gurung managed one yuko and two ippon.

Other Nepali karate contenders also endured a dismal outing despite coming close to the podium. In men's kumite, Min Bahadur Tamang (under-60kg) and Rakesh Manandhar (under-55kg) both missed out on bronze medals. Tamang advanced past Hong Kong's Ka Him Chau (4-1) and Tajikistan's Muhammad Mirzozoda (2-0) before losing his semi-final 10-0 to Kuwait's Abdullah Shaaban. He subsequently lost his bronze-medal bout 2-0 to Saudi Arabia's Saud Abdulaziz Albasher.

Manandhar suffered a one-sided 7-0 semi-final defeat to Uzbekistan's Khalimov Khumoyunmirzo, having earlier booked his place in the last four with a 9-0 win over Thailand's Natthakrit Ingloy. He then missed the bronze after falling 9-1 to Malaysia's Thevendran Kaliana Sundram. In women's kata, Sanu Maya Thing was beaten 5-0 in the round of 16 by South Korea's Haeun Choi.

Despite the setbacks, Nepal Karate Federation President Yuba Raj Lama praised the team's efforts. "We could not achieve our target in Nagoya and missed three bronze-medal opportunities. This is an important lesson for us. We still have three matches remaining and remain hopeful of giving our best," Lama posted on social media. Nepal has three matches left in the karate competition.

Volleyball

The Nepali women's volleyball team concluded their Nagoya campaign with a single victory, defeating Kyrgyzstan in straight sets. Following group-stage losses to hosts Japan and Indonesia, Nepal entered the classification play-offs for the 9th to 14th positions.

Nepal registered a 25-20, 25-16, 25-20 win over Kyrgyzstan, wrapping up the match in one hour and eight minutes.

Table Tennis

Nepal's table tennis teams mirrored the struggles of their compatriots, with both the men's and women's squads starting their group matches with defeats.

The men's team, comprising Rubin Maharjan, Sanyog Kapali, and Gananjaya Dahal, lost in straight sets to Chinese Taipei. Maharjan went down to Yun-ju Lin (11-5, 11-1, 11-7), Kapali lost to Jing-kai Hung (11-5, 11-5, 11-4), and Dahal was defeated 11-3, 11-2, 11-0. The team will face Bahrain in their next Group C fixture.

In the women's event, Nepal proved no match for table tennis powerhouse China, losing in straight sets. Evana Thapa fell to Yi Chen (11-1, 11-6, 11-5), Nabita Shrestha lost to Man Kuai (11-4, 11-3, 11-4), and Yonggi Poudel was beaten by Shuhan Fan (11-1, 11-5, 11-1). The Nepali women will next face Macau, China.

Wushu

Wushu athletes faced a similarly difficult outing. Bijaya Sinjali, who won a bronze medal at the 3rd Taolu World Cup, finished 19th out of 21 competitors in the men's changquan event with 9.146 points.

In the women's taijiquan, Sabita Rai was placed 11th with 8.653 points. Rai also finished tenth in the taijijian final held at the Aichi Prefectural Hall on Sunday, scoring 9.183 points.

title: China indefinitely closes Tatopani checkpoint on Nepal border — Kathmandu Post - ua.news
description: China indefinitely closes Tatopani checkpoint on Nepal border — Kathmandu Post  ua.news
publisher.title: ua.news
full_article:
China has indefinitely closed the Tatopani border checkpoint on its border with Nepal since August 29, citing the risk of landslides on the Nepalese side. At the same time, trade through the Rasuwagadhi checkpoint has come to a complete halt following the destructive floods of the Bhotekoshi River last month. As The Kathmandu Post reports, the restrictions are complicating the supply of goods from China ahead of Nepalese festivals Dashain, Tihar and Chhath.

Delays and higher transportation costs

The Korala checkpoint in Upper Mustang, which remains an available route for imports, does not have sufficient resources for the seasonal load. Due to poor road conditions, delivering goods from the border to their destinations takes longer and costs more.

Traders who have already lost cargo due to the floods are facing additional transportation costs and supply delays. This is also affecting retail prices for consumers. The publication notes that during the holiday period, some unscrupulous sellers may artificially raise prices.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Negotiations on restoring the route

In its editorial, The Kathmandu Post calls on Nepalese authorities to continue negotiations with Beijing on restoring Tatopani's operations and to pay attention to the Arniko Highway, which connects the checkpoint with Kathmandu. According to traders and customs officials, the road is currently suitable for cargo traffic despite minor landslides.

Nepal has also asked China for assistance in rebuilding the 16-kilometer Syaphrubesi-Rasuwagadhi road damaged by flooding. In the previous fiscal year, Nepal imported goods worth 425.24 billion rupees from China, while imports worth 47.48 billion rupees passed through Tatopani.

After the 2015 earthquakes, Tatopani was closed for nearly four years, and the checkpoint's operations were also suspended during the COVID-19 pandemic. The publication emphasizes the need to develop reliable, disaster-resilient trade routes in the Himalayan direction that can operate throughout the year.

title: Number of humanities students declining in Nepal — Kathmandu Post - ua.news
description: Number of humanities students declining in Nepal — Kathmandu Post  ua.news
publisher.title: ua.news
full_article:
In Nepal, the number of high school students taking examinations in sociology, psychology and mass communications is rapidly declining. At the same time, the number of examinees in physics, biology, chemistry, accounting and economics is increasing. As reported by Kathmandu Post, data from the National Examination Board also indicate a decrease in the number of schools offering humanities subjects.

Decline in student numbers

In the 2022/23 academic year, 14,473 students took the Grade 12 sociology examination, 605 took psychology, and 4,403 took mass communications. In the 2025/26 academic year, these figures fell to 9,004, 202 and 2,469, respectively.

Over the same period, the number of physics examinees increased from 52,370 to 60,939, biology examinees from 32,147 to 39,125, and chemistry examinees from 52,355 to 60,923. The accounting examination was taken by 174,771 students in 2022/23 and 185,027 in 2025/26. The number of students taking economics rose from 167,619 to 169,862.

Schools abandon programs

The number of schools offering sociology decreased from 586 to 398 during this period. Psychology was offered by 24 schools in the 2022/23 academic year and by 16 in 2025/26. History was offered by only eight schools in the latter of these academic years.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Indira K C, a sociology teacher and chief academic adviser at United Academy, noted that students consider the science stream more universal for further education, while the opportunities offered by humanities disciplines remain insufficiently explored. Suresh Gautam, an associate professor at the Kathmandu University School of Education, linked the trend to the perception of education primarily as a tool for increasing income.

Focus on high-paying careers

According to Gautam, the school system is largely focused on results and grades, leaving little time for reading, writing and independent thinking beyond the curriculum. Mukunda Raj Sharma, director of Little Angels’ School, acknowledged that humanities subjects could at least be available as electives, but said they do not attract sufficient interest among most parents, students or in the market.

According to Merina Shakya Bajracharya, who is responsible for the Grade 11–12 program at St Mary’s School, the school cancelled its humanities program this year because of the small number of students. She said the group size had never exceeded 20 people, and only six students were enrolled in it last year.

description: Nepal Floods Leave Survivors Searching for Lost Homes and Loved Ones  India News Network
publisher.title: India News Network
full_article: In Nepal, catastrophic flooding has displaced thousands of residents, prompting survivors to navigate through the remnants of their former lives as they search for lost family members and belongings. One survivor, Anusa Thapa Magar, returned from her job in the Maldives, hoping to find her grandmother alive. However, when she arrived in Betrawati, the family’s hometown, she was met with a barren landscape of hardened grey silt, devoid of any traces of their former residence. Anusa, 23, expressed her despair, questioning if her grandmother might still be beneath the rubble of their home, which was built to accommodate her grandmother's mobility issues. "If my house is buried underneath, that means my Aama is still here underneath too, right?" she said quietly. The flooding was triggered by a glacial collapse in the mountains bordering Nepal and China, resulting in significant devastation along the Trishuli River. Authorities have reported at least 1,386 fatalities on the Nepalese side, with 5,130 individuals currently unaccounted for. Despite ongoing search efforts, there have been no recent discoveries of survivors. To reach what was once Betrawati, residents must traverse steep hills and narrow ridges, an arduous journey revealing scattered personal items like shoes and children's backpacks, which testify to the urgency of the evacuation as the floodwaters surged. Kalpana Thapa Magar, a 43-year-old garment business owner, recounted her experience during the disaster when she received a frantic call from a friend. "Run! Run!" was the advice that prompted her to flee, and when she turned back, she found everything gone, including others who had been fleeing alongside her. In the downstream area of Devighat, the shells of houses remain standing, with some residents sifting through the rubble to reclaim what little they can. Many however, claim there is no reason to return as the land is now buried under debris. This disaster conjures painful memories of the 2015 earthquake that claimed nearly 9,000 lives in Nepal. Sita Thapa Magar, a teacher and Kalpana’s older sister, lamented, "This time, we have lost everything. Our houses, our land, our future." Shanti Dangol, 61, found herself holding onto a broken floor tile—one of the last remnants of her three-storey lodge that once accommodated trekkers and pilgrims. "Economically, people here had started doing well. Now, nothing remains," she said, reflecting on the community's previous recovery efforts and current despair.

title: Sharon Verma to perform in Nepal for the first time — Kathmandu Post - ua.news
description: Sharon Verma to perform in Nepal for the first time — Kathmandu Post  ua.news
publisher.title: ua.news
full_article:
Indian stand-up comedian and writer Sharon Verma will perform in Nepal for the first time on September 27, 2026. Her show, Sharon Verma Live, will take place at Nepal Academy Hall in the Kamaladi district of Kathmandu and will begin at 16:30.

Performance in Kathmandu

The event is organized by Pinnacle Entertainment. The project's strategic consultant is Yash Bharadwaj. Tickets for the performance are available through the Khalti service.

As Kathmandu Post reports, the performance in Kathmandu will be Verma's first live appearance in Nepal. The show will take place at one of the country's capital's notable concert venues.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

The comedian's style

Verma is known for her observational and self-deprecating style of humor. She gained broader recognition after appearing on India’s Got Latent: her performance and the Weak Independent Woman persona were widely discussed online.

After that, the comedian continued performing stand-up in India and developing her audience through live shows and digital content.

full_article:
Among those missing are 636 foreign nationals. Rasuwa and Nuwakot remain among the worst-affected districts, with thousands of locals and non-locals still unaccounted for.

Authorities have rescued 13,784 people, while more than 20,900 security personnel are involved in ongoing search and rescue operations.

Meanwhile, 1,231 displaced people are staying at 20 holding centers.

Authorities have also collected DNA samples to help identify victims, including 530 unidentified remains.

Earlier, Qazinform reported rapid warming in the Himalayas was increasing the risk of rock collapses, rock-ice avalanches and subsequent floods that could overwhelm existing protective measures, according to a study by World Weather Attribution.
